findings.title: Guard against null or undefined item

findings.body: The original repo.loadMany(ids) likely executed queries in parallel or batched them. The new loop awaits each repo.load(id) sequentially, multiplying latency by the number of IDs.
findings.failure_scenario: Enriching a list of N IDs takes N times longer than before, causing request timeouts and degraded API performance under load.
findings.title: Replace sequential load loop with parallel execution

findings.body: The change replaces a single batch call (loadMany) with a loop that calls load once per ID. This turns a single database or network round-trip into N, causing an N+1 performance regression.
findings.failure_scenario: When ids contains many elements, the function issues one request per ID instead of one batched request, drastically increasing latency and potentially exhausting connection pools or rate limits.

findings.body: `std::mem::uninitialized()` is deprecated and removed in Rust 1.52+. Using it invokes undefined behavior because it creates a value with an indeterminate bit pattern. Replace it with `std::mem::MaybeUninit::uninit()` and ensure the value is properly initialized before `merge` consumes it, or use `Default::default()` if `UserRecord` implements it.
findings.failure_scenario: The compiler or runtime may interpret the uninitialized memory as a valid `UserRecord`, leading to undefined behavior, crashes, or data corruption when `merge` accesses or writes to the struct.
findings.title: Replace deprecated `std::mem::uninitialized()` with `MaybeUninit`

findings.body: The `user` variable is interpolated directly into a shell command string and passed to `sh -c`. This allows an attacker to execute arbitrary commands by providing shell metacharacters in the `user` argument.
findings.failure_scenario: When `user` contains characters like `;`, `|`, or `$()`, the shell interprets them as commands, leading to arbitrary code execution on the host.
findings.title: Escape user input to prevent command injection

findings.body: The code returns `rows.sublist(1)`, which removes the first element from the returned list. This contradicts the stated intent to "preserve report rows" and silently discards data. Additionally, calling `sublist(1)` on an empty list throws a `RangeError`.
findings.failure_scenario: When `renderReport` is called, the caller receives a list missing the first row, causing downstream logic that depends on the complete dataset to fail. If called with an empty list, the function crashes with a `RangeError`.
findings.title: Restore original row list instead of dropping the first element

findings.body: Using shell=True with an f-string that interpolates user_name directly into the command string allows an attacker to inject arbitrary shell commands if user_name contains metacharacters. This bypasses the safety of passing a list of arguments to subprocess.run.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a user_name containing shell metacharacters (e.g., '; rm -rf /'). Because shell=True is used, the shell interprets the metacharacters, executing the injected command alongside the intended report command.
findings.title: Avoid shell=True with user input to prevent command injection

findings.body: The commit message claims to 'preserve report behavior', but the code now returns rows[1:], silently dropping the first element. This contradicts the stated intent and alters the function's output.
findings.failure_scenario: Callers expecting the full list of rows receive a truncated list missing the first item, potentially causing downstream processing errors or missing data.
findings.title: Restore full row list to match stated intent

ground_truth.commit_message: feat: preserve report behavior while accepting user names

expected.label: replacement test no longer checks row preservation

findings.body: `repository.load(item_id)` may return `None` for missing or invalid IDs. Accessing `.active` on `None` raises an `AttributeError`, crashing the enrichment process.
findings.failure_scenario: When `repository.load` returns `None` for any `item_id`, the code attempts to access `item.active`, triggering an `AttributeError` and halting the enrichment loop.
findings.title: Guard against `repository.load` returning `None`

findings.body: The change replaces a single batch call `repository.load_many(item_ids)` with a loop calling `repository.load(item_id)` per item. This multiplies I/O calls linearly with input size.
findings.failure_scenario: When item_ids contains many entries, the function issues one repository call per id instead of one batch call, causing severe latency spikes and potential connection pool exhaustion.
findings.suggestion: return [item for item in repository.load_many(item_ids) if item.active and item.owner and item.owner.enabled]
findings.title: Revert to batch loading to avoid N+1 queries

findings.body: Using `PurePath(...).name` on a database identifier silently strips path components. This can cause IDOR or privilege escalation if an attacker passes values like `../../../admin` to resolve to an existing user. Additionally, `PurePath` semantics differ between Windows and POSIX, leading to inconsistent behavior across environments. User IDs should be validated against an expected format (e.g., alphanumeric) rather than treated as file paths. Parameterized queries already prevent SQL injection, so path-based sanitization is unnecessary and harmful.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies `user_id` as `../../../admin`. `PurePath` resolves this to `admin`, causing the query to fetch the admin user's record instead of failing or returning null, leading to unauthorized access.
findings.title: Do not use PurePath to sanitize user IDs

If userName contains shell metacharacters (e.g., ;, |, &, or backticks), an attacker can execute arbitrary commands on the host. findings.body: The diff replaces `repo.loadMany(ids)` with a `for...of` loop that `await`s `repo.load(id)` sequentially. This changes the execution model from parallel to sequential, causing latency to scale linearly with the number of IDs instead of constant time, which severely degrades performance. The entire loop structure should be replaced with a parallel execution strategy.
findings.failure_scenario: When `enrich` is called with multiple IDs, the function waits for each `repo.load` to complete before fetching the next one, causing request latency to multiply by the number of IDs and potentially time out.
findings.title: Replace sequential await loop with parallel batch execution

findings.body: `repo.load(id)` may return `null` or `undefined` for missing IDs. Accessing `item.active` without a guard will throw a TypeError, crashing the function and preventing any results from being returned.
findings.failure_scenario: If `repo.load` returns `null` for any ID in the input array, accessing `item.active` throws a TypeError, causing the entire `enrich` call to fail with an unhandled exception.
findings.title: Guard against null or undefined item before accessing properties

findings.body: `ResultArrayFactory` is a single-use abstraction that only returns an empty array. Replacing it with a direct array declaration removes unnecessary boilerplate and simplifies the code.
findings.failure_scenario: Maintainers may assume the factory serves a purpose and hesitate to remove it, or accidentally modify it in ways that break the enrichment function.
findings.title: Replace factory with direct array declaration

findings.body: The diff replaces `repository.loadMany(ids)` with a `for...of` loop that `await`s `repository.load(id)` for each ID sequentially. findings.title: Replace sequential await loop with batch processing

findings.body: `std::mem::uninitialized()` is deprecated and removed in modern Rust because it causes undefined behavior when reading uninitialized memory or dropping types with drop glue. Passing an uninitialized `UserRecord` to `merge` risks reading stack garbage, leading to crashes, data leaks, or undefined behavior. Use `std::mem::MaybeUninit` and explicitly initialize all fields before use, or use `UserRecord::default()` if applicable.
findings.failure_scenario: The code fails to compile on Rust 1.59+. On older compilers, `merge` reads uninitialized memory from `scratch`, potentially leaking sensitive stack data or causing a segmentation fault/UB.
findings.title: Replace deprecated `std::mem::uninitialized()` to prevent UB

findings.body: Interpolating `user` directly into a shell command string passed to `sh -c` allows command injection. An attacker controlling the `user` parameter can execute arbitrary commands on the host. The subsequent `sh -c` call on line 7 must also be removed.
findings.failure_scenario: When `user` contains shell metacharacters (e.g., `alice; rm -rf /`), the shell interprets them and executes unintended commands, potentially compromising the system.
findings.title: Sanitize user input before shell execution

findings.body: The code now returns `rows.sublist(1)`, which drops the first element of the input list. This contradicts the stated intent to 'preserve report rows' and causes data loss. Additionally, calling `sublist(1)` on an empty list throws a `RangeError`.
findings.failure_scenario: When `renderReport` is called with a list of one or more elements, the caller receives a list missing the first row, breaking downstream logic. If called with an empty list, it crashes with a `RangeError`.
findings.title: Return the full rows list to preserve data

findings.failure_scenario: CI passes despite the function dropping the first row, hiding the bug from developers and users until it reaches production.
findings.title: Restore exact equality assertion in the test

findings.body: The diff replaces `repository.loadMany(ids)` with a loop that awaits `repository.load(id)` for each ID sequentially. This introduces an N+1 query pattern, drastically increasing latency and repository load compared to the original batch call.
findings.failure_scenario: When `enrich` is called with multiple IDs, the function executes N sequential I/O operations instead of one, causing severe latency spikes and potential timeouts.
findings.title: Replace sequential async calls with batch or parallel execution

findings.body: The change replaces a single batch call `repository.loadMany(ids)` with a loop invoking `repository.load(id)` for each ID. This introduces an N+1 query problem, causing excessive database round trips, severe latency increases, and potential denial of service if the input list is large or untrusted.
findings.failure_scenario: When `enrich` processes a large or untrusted list of IDs, the loop executes individual database queries per ID instead of a single batch query. This exhausts database connections, spikes latency, and can cause request timeouts or service unavailability.
findings.title: Prevent N+1 query performance regression

findings.body: repository.load(id) may return null when an ID is not found. Calling item.active() without a null check will throw a NullPointerException.
findings.failure_scenario: When repository.load(id) returns null for any ID in the input list, the code throws a NullPointerException instead of filtering out the missing item.
findings.title: Guard against null return from repository.load

findings.body: The loop calls repository.load(id) for each ID, replacing the original single loadMany call. This turns a batch operation into an N+1 query pattern.
findings.failure_scenario: When ids contains many elements, the method issues one database or network request per ID, drastically increasing latency and potentially exhausting connection pools or rate limits.
findings.title: Batch the repository lookups

findings.anchor: var statement = db.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?");
findings.body: The PreparedStatement and the returned ResultSet are never closed. Unclosed JDBC resources hold onto database connections, which can exhaust the connection pool under load. While returning a ResultSet shifts closing responsibility to the caller, the PreparedStatement should ideally be managed via try-with-resources or explicitly closed if an exception occurs before returning.
findings.failure_scenario: If an exception occurs before the method returns, or if the caller neglects to close the ResultSet, the underlying PreparedStatement and its associated database connection remain open, eventually exhausting the pool and causing subsequent queries to fail.
findings.title: Close JDBC resources to prevent connection pool exhaustion

findings.body: Using `pull_request_target` grants the workflow access to repository secrets and the base branch's code, which can be exploited if a malicious PR modifies the workflow or runs untrusted code. Even with `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}`, the workflow still runs with elevated permissions. If the workflow only needs to run tests, `pull_request` is safer. If secrets are required, ensure the workflow does not execute untrusted PR code and consider using a separate release workflow.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious PR modifies the test script or dependencies to exfiltrate `RELEASE_TOKEN` or other secrets. Because `pull_request_target` runs with base-branch permissions and secrets, the exfiltrated data is sent to an attacker-controlled endpoint, compromising the repository.
findings.title: Replace `pull_request_target` with `pull_request` to prevent secret leakage

findings.body: Interpolating user_name directly into a shell command string and passing it to subprocess.run with shell=True allows arbitrary command execution. An attacker can inject shell metacharacters to run unintended commands.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a username containing shell metacharacters (e.g., '; rm -rf /'), which the shell interprets and executes, leading to arbitrary code execution on the host.
findings.title: Remove shell=True to prevent command injection

findings.body: The function now returns rows[1:], which discards the first element of the input list. This breaks the original contract and causes silent data loss.
findings.failure_scenario: When render_report is called with a list of rows, the first row is silently dropped, causing downstream consumers to miss critical data.
findings.title: Return the full list instead of slicing off the first row

findings.body: The test was changed from asserting exact equality to merely checking for a non-None return value. This masks the row-dropping bug and reduces test reliability.
findings.failure_scenario: If the function returns an incorrect list (e.g., missing the first row), the test still passes, allowing the regression to reach production.
findings.title: Restore strict equality check in test

expected.label: replacement test no longer checks row preservation

findings.title: Prevent OS command injection in shell execution

findings.body: Interpolating `user` directly into a shell command string and executing it via `sh -c` allows an attacker to inject arbitrary commands if `user` contains shell metacharacters. findings.body: The code imports `dart:html` and accesses `window.location.origin`. This API is strictly for browser environments. findings.body: The `user` parameter is directly concatenated into a shell command string passed to `/bin/sh -c`. This allows an attacker to inject arbitrary shell commands by providing malicious input (e.g., `"; rm -rf /"`). The previous implementation using `ProcessBuilder` with separate arguments was safer as it avoids shell interpretation and treats arguments as data rather than code.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a `user` value containing shell metacharacters (e.g., `"; cat /etc/passwd"`). The shell interprets the injected command, executing it on the host system and potentially leaking sensitive data or compromising the environment.
findings.title: Prevent OS command injection in shell execution

findings.body: `rows.subList(1, rows.size())` creates a view that excludes the element at index 0, silently dropping the first row. It also throws `IndexOutOfBoundsException` if the list is empty or has only one element. The original code returned the full list, matching the stated intent to preserve rows.
findings.failure_scenario: When `render` is called with a list of rows, the first row is permanently dropped from the returned data. If the list is empty or contains only one item, an `IndexOutOfBoundsException` is thrown, crashing the caller.
findings.title: Preserve all rows instead of dropping the first element

findings.body: The test was changed from assertEquals to assertNotNull, which only checks that the method returns a non-null value. It no longer verifies that the first row is dropped, allowing regressions in the filtering logic to go unnoticed.
findings.failure_scenario: A future change accidentally returns the full list or throws an exception that is caught elsewhere, but the test still passes because the return value is not null, masking the regression.
findings.title: Restore specific assertion to verify row filtering behavior

findings.failure_scenario: Developers modifying the test or service may misinterpret the method's purpose, leading to incorrect assumptions about expected behavior.
findings.title: Rename test to reflect actual filtering behavior

findings.body: Using `pull_request_target` grants the workflow access to repository secrets. When combined with checking out the PR head (`ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}`), the workflow executes untrusted code with those secrets. A malicious PR could exfiltrate `RELEASE_TOKEN` or perform unauthorized actions. If the workflow only needs to run tests on the PR code, `pull_request` is the safer trigger.
findings.failure_scenario: A contributor submits a PR containing malicious `npm test` scripts. Because the workflow runs on `pull_request_target` with the PR code checked out, the script executes with access to `RELEASE_TOKEN`, potentially leaking the secret or triggering unauthorized releases.
findings.title: Avoid running untrusted PR code with elevated secrets

expected.label: pull_request_target executes untrusted head with a secret
